questions.question: If a pilot views an object directly at night, how does the "night blind spot" affect visibility as the distance to the object increases?
questions.correct_answer: It can hide larger objects that would otherwise be visible.
distractors: It becomes less effective, making larger objects easier to see at a distance.
It only affects small objects, leaving larger objects clearly visible regardless of distance.
It shifts the blind spot from central vision to peripheral vision as distance increases.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, the night blind spot is caused by the absence of rods in the fovea, affecting the central 5 to 10 degrees of the visual field. When an object is viewed directly at night, it may go undetected or fade away. Specifically, the night blind spot can hide larger objects as the distance between the pilot and the object increases.

reference.text:
The “Night Blind Spot” appears under conditions of low ambient illumination due to the absence of rods in the fovea. [Figure 11-3]
This absence of rods affects the central 5 to 10 degrees of the visual field. If an object is viewed directly at night, it may go
undetected or it may fade away after initial detection. The night blind spot can hide larger objects as the distance between the pilot
and an object increases.

questions.question: While turning to final at night, approach lights create an illusion that makes the aircraft appear higher than it actually is. If a pilot reacts to this illusion, what is the most likely dangerous outcome?
questions.correct_answer: The pilot may descend prematurely, resulting in an approach that is dangerously low
distractors: The pilot may climb unnecessarily, resulting in an approach that is too high
The pilot may level the wings early to eliminate the illusion, causing runway misalignment
The pilot may mistake approach lights for runway boundary lights and land long
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, under certain conditions, approach lights can make the aircraft seem higher in a turn to final than when its wings are level. This illusion creates a false perception of being too high. If the pilot trusts this visual cue and descends based on it, they will fly an approach that is lower than intended, potentially creating a hazardous situation. The other options are incorrect because a pilot perceiving themselves as too high would not climb, would not level wings to fix a height illusion, and while confusing approach and runway lights is a separate problem mentioned in the same section, it is a different issue from the height illusion described.

reference.text:
Illusions created by runway lights result in a variety of problems. Bright lights or bold colors advance the runway, making it appear
closer. Night landings are further complicated by the difficulty of judging distance and the possibility of confusing approach and
runway lights. For example, when a double row of approach lights joins the boundary lights of the runway, there can be confusion as
to where the approach lights terminate and runway lights begin. Under certain conditions, approach lights can make the aircraft seem
higher in a turn to final, than when its wings are level.

questions.question: A pilot is approaching an airport at night and notices the runway lights are already illuminated. Why should the pilot still key the microphone when overflying the airport or just prior to entering the final approach segment?
questions.correct_answer: To confirm the aircraft is close enough to activate the system and ensure a full 15-minute lighting duration is available
distractors: To extinguish the previously activated lights and restart the 15-minute timer with a fresh activation cycle
To cycle the runway edge lights from aviation yellow to aviation white, indicating the runway is active for landing
To test whether the airport's radio-controlled lighting receiver is set to low or high sensitivity mode
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, radio-controlled lighting receivers may be set at a low sensitivity due to the close proximity of airports using the same frequency, requiring the aircraft to be relatively close to activate the system. Even if lights appear to already be on, keying the mike when overflying or entering the final segment ensures the aircraft is close enough to activate the system and that a full 15-minute lighting duration is available from that most recent activation. The lights cannot be extinguished prior to the end of a 15-minute period, so the distractor about extinguishing and restarting is incorrect. Runway edge light colors (white and yellow) are fixed and not pilot-selectable, and the system is not used to test receiver sensitivity.

reference.text:
The basic runway lighting system consists of two straight parallel lines of runway edge lights defining the lateral limits of the runway.
These lights are aviation white, although aviation yellow may be substituted for a distance of 2,000 feet from the far end of the
runway to indicate a caution zone. At some airports, the intensity of the runway edge lights can be activated and adjusted by radio
control. The control system consists of a 3-step control responsive to 7, 5, and/or 3 microphone clicks. This 3-step control turns on
lighting facilities capable of either 3-step, 2-step, or 1-step operation. The 3-step and 2-step lighting facilities can be altered in
intensity, while the 1-step cannot. All lighting is illuminated for a period of 15 minutes from the most recent time of activation and
may not be extinguished prior to end of the 15-minute period. Suggested use is to always initially key the mike 7 times; this assures
that all controlled lights are turned on to the maximum available intensity. If desired, adjustment can then be made, where the
capability is provided, to a lower intensity by keying 5 and/or 3 times. Due to the close proximity of airports using the same
frequency, radio-controlled lighting receivers may be set at a low sensitivity requiring the aircraft to be relatively close to activate the
system. Consequently, even when lights are on, the pilot should always key the mike as directed when overflying an airport of
intended landing or just prior to entering the final segment of an approach. This assures the aircraft is close enough to activate the
system and a full 15-minute lighting duration is available.

questions.question: A VFR pilot on a cross-country flight unexpectedly encounters instrument meteorological conditions (IMC). According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, under what circumstances does the risk associated with this situation increase dramatically?
questions.correct_answer: Unless the pilot and aircraft are both equipped for IFR flight and an IFR flight plan has been prepared and filed that can be activated if needed
distractors: Unless the pilot has received a standard weather briefing within the past 24 hours and has a VFR flight plan on file
Unless the aircraft is equipped with a functioning autopilot and the pilot has completed an instrument proficiency check within the last 6 calendar months
Unless the pilot immediately contacts ATC to request VFR flight following and begins a 180-degree turn to reverse course
questions.explanation: The Airplane Flying Handbook (Chapter 11, Orientation and Navigation) states that if encountering IMC, risk increases dramatically unless both the pilot and aircraft are equipped for flight under IFR, and the pilot has prepared and filed an IFR flight plan that can be activated if needed. This emphasizes that all three conditions must be met: pilot qualification, aircraft equipment, and a filed IFR flight plan. A VFR flight plan, VFR flight following, or having received a weather briefing do not substitute for these requirements. An autopilot alone does not constitute being 'equipped for IFR flight' for the pilot, and contacting ATC for flight following is not the same as having an IFR flight plan on file.

reference.text:
Generally, at night, it is difficult to see clouds and restrictions to visibility, particularly on dark nights or under an overcast. When
flying under VFR, pilots should exercise caution to avoid flying into clouds. Usually, the first indication of flying into restricted
visibility conditions is the gradual disappearance of lights on the ground. If the lights begin to appear surrounded by a halo or glow,
further flight in the same direction calls for caution. Such a halo or glow around lights on the ground is indicative of ground fog. If a
descent occurs through clouds, smoke, or haze in order to land, the horizontal visibility is considerably less when looking through the
restriction than it is when looking straight down through it from above. Pilots should avoid a VFR night flight if expecting conditions
below VFR minimums. If encountering IMC, risk increases dramatically unless both the pilot and aircraft are equipped for flight
under IFR, and the pilot has prepared and filed an IFR flight plan that can be activated, if needed.

questions.question: While a clear night generally provides good visibility, what specific visual hazard can make it difficult to identify the horizon when flying over a large body of water?
questions.correct_answer: Stars reflected on the water surface can appear as a continuous array of lights.
distractors: The water absorbs the starlight, causing the water and sky to blend into a single dark mass.
Reflected starlight creates a flickering optical illusion on the water that induces vertigo.
Ambient starlight reduces the contrast between the water surface and distant shorelines.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, even on clear nights over water, stars may be reflected on the water's surface. This reflection can appear as a continuous array of lights, which makes the horizon difficult to identify and can lead to a loss of orientation.

reference.text:
Crossing large bodies of water at night in single-engine airplanes could be potentially hazardous, because in the event of an
engine failure, the pilot may be forced to land (ditch) the airplane in the water. Another hazard faced by pilots of all aircraft, due to
limited or no lighting, is that the horizon blends with the water. During poor visibility conditions over water, the horizon becomes
obscure and may result in a loss of orientation. Even on clear nights, the stars may be reflected on the water surface, which
could appear as a continuous array of lights, thus making the horizon difficult to identify.

questions.question: During a night approach, the landing light may be ineffective at higher altitudes and can even reflect glare back into the pilot's eyes in hazy or foggy conditions. Despite these disadvantages, what is a valid reason to still turn it on?
questions.correct_answer: Safety considerations regarding local traffic and collision avoidance may outweigh the disadvantages
distractors: The landing light beam effectively illuminates the runway surface from any altitude, improving landing accuracy
The landing light is required by regulation to be activated whenever the airplane is on final approach at night
The landing light enhances the pilot's depth perception during the roundout and flare
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, the landing light is usually turned on halfway through the final approach during night operations. The handbook acknowledges that the light beam may not reach the ground from higher altitudes and may be reflected back into the pilot's eyes by haze, smoke, or fog. However, safety considerations regarding local traffic and collision avoidance may overshadow these disadvantages, meaning the benefit of being seen by other aircraft can justify using the light despite its drawbacks.

reference.text:
After turning onto the final approach and aligning the airplane midway between the two rows of runway-edge lights, the pilot should
note and correct for any wind drift. Throughout the final approach, proper use of pitch and power helps to maintain a stabilized
approach. Flaps are used as in a normal approach. Usually, halfway through the final approach, the landing light is turned on. The
landing light is sometimes ineffective since the light beam will usually not reach the ground from higher altitudes. The light may even
be reflected back into the pilot’s eyes by any existing haze, smoke, or fog. Safety considerations regarding local traffic and collision
avoidance may overshadow these disadvantages. 11-10

questions.question: When executing a night landing without landing lights, what technique should a pilot use during the round out and touchdown to safely reach the runway surface?
questions.correct_answer: Feel for the runway surface using power and pitch changes, allowing the airplane to settle slowly to the runway
distractors: Maintain a constant approach descent rate all the way to the runway without rounding out, since visual references are unavailable
Rely solely on the attitude indicator to determine pitch and power settings during touchdown
Keep the approach airspeed constant and flare aggressively once the runway edge lights disappear below the cowling
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, during landings without the use of landing lights, the round out may be started when the runway lights at the far end of the runway first appear to be rising higher than the nose of the airplane. This demands a smooth and very timely round out and requires that the pilot feel for the runway surface using power and pitch changes, as necessary, for the airplane to settle slowly to the runway. The scarcity of observable objects at night impairs judgment of height, speed, and sink rate, making this tactile technique essential for a safe touchdown.

reference.text:
The round out and touchdown is made in the same manner as in day landings. At night, the judgment of height, speed, and sink rate is
impaired by the scarcity of observable objects in the landing area. An inexperienced pilot may have a tendency to round out too high.
Continuing a constant approach descent until the landing lights reflect on the runway and tire marks on the runway can be seen clearly
helps identify the point to begin the round out. At this point, the round out is started smoothly and the throttle gradually reduced to
idle as the airplane is touching down. [Figure 11-8] During landings without the use of landing lights, the round out may be started
when the runway lights at the far end of the runway first appear to be rising higher than the nose of the airplane. This demands a
smooth and very timely round out and requires that the pilot feel for the runway surface using power and pitch changes, as necessary,
for the airplane to settle slowly to the runway. Blackout landings should always be included in night pilot training as an emergency
procedure. 11-11 11-12

questions.question: During a night emergency landing, your landing lights are inoperative and you have no outside visual references. What should you do as the airplane descends toward the surface?
questions.correct_answer: Hold the airplane in a level-landing attitude until the ground is contacted
distractors: Execute a full-stall landing just above the surface to minimize impact force
Increase airspeed slightly and land flat to reduce the chance of a nose-first impact
Pitch down slightly to ensure contact with the ground as soon as possible
Flare aggressively at the estimated moment of touchdown
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, Night Emergencies, if the landing lights are unusable and outside visual references are not available, the airplane should be held in a level-landing attitude until the ground is contacted. Attempting to judge flare height without visual references is impossible, so maintaining a level-landing attitude is the safest option. A full-stall landing or aggressive flare requires precise height judgment that is unavailable, increasing airspeed contradicts the goal of touching down at the slowest possible airspeed, and pitching down risks a nose-first impact.

reference.text:
⦁ Complete the before-landing checklist, and check the landing lights for operation at altitude and turn ON in
      sufficient time to illuminate the terrain or obstacles along the flightpath. The landing should be completed
      in the normal landing attitude at the slowest possible airspeed. If the landing lights are unusable and outside
      visual references are not available, the airplane should be held in level-landing attitude until the ground is
      contacted.

questions.question: A student pilot claims that night flight requires different control inputs because the airplane responds differently in darkness. How should an instructor correct this misconception?
questions.correct_answer: The airplane performs and responds to control inputs the same as during the day; it is the pilot who is affected by various physical limitations and operational considerations at night
distractors: The airplane's control effectiveness is reduced at night due to decreased air density, requiring the pilot to use larger control inputs
The airplane's engine produces less power at night due to cooler temperatures, so the pilot must adjust throttle settings accordingly
The airplane's instruments and systems operate at reduced sensitivity in darkness, requiring the pilot to interpret readings differently than during the day
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, the mechanical operation of an airplane at night is no different than during the day. The airplane does not know if it is being operated in the dark or in bright sunlight—it performs and responds to control inputs by the pilot the same way. It is the pilot who is affected by various aspects of night operations, including actual physical limitations as well as considerations such as equipment requirements, procedures, and emergency situations.

reference.text:
Introduction
The mechanical operation of an airplane at night is no different than operating the same airplane during the day. The airplane does not
know if it is being operated in the dark or in bright sunlight. It performs and responds to control inputs by the pilot. The
pilot, however, is affected by various aspects of night operations and should take them into consideration during night flight
operations. Some are actual physical limitations affecting all pilots. Others, such as equipment requirements, procedures, and
emergency situations, should also be considered.

questions.question: While the mechanical operation and performance of an airplane remain the same at night as they do during the day, which of the following factors must a pilot specifically consider when planning for and conducting night flight operations?
questions.correct_answer: Physical limitations, equipment requirements, procedures, and emergency situations
distractors: Changes in aircraft performance, engine operating temperatures, and fuel consumption rates
Aerodynamic changes, control input delays, and modified center of gravity
Altered fuel-to-air mixtures, magneto timing, and spark plug fouling
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) Chapter 11, the airplane itself does not know if it is being operated in the dark or in bright sunlight and performs the same. However, the pilot is affected by various aspects of night operations and must take into consideration actual physical limitations, equipment requirements, procedures, and emergency situations.

questions.question: A pilot is reviewing whether an early morning flight should be logged as night flying time. To make this determination, the pilot needs to understand when morning civil twilight begins and ends. Which statement is correct?
questions.correct_answer: Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunrise.
distractors: Morning civil twilight begins at sunrise and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon.
Morning civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon.
Morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ends at sunset.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook Chapter 11, the National Weather Service defines morning civil twilight as beginning when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon and ending at sunrise. This is distinct from evening civil twilight, which begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. Since 14 CFR part 1 defines 'night' as the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, a pilot must understand these boundaries to accurately determine if a flight occurred during night conditions. Distractor 1 reverses the beginning and end points; Distractor 2 describes evening civil twilight; Distractor 3 incorrectly uses sunset as the ending point rather than sunrise.

reference.text:
According to 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1, Definitions and Abbreviations, “night” means the time between the end of evening civil
twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. To explain further, the
National Weather Service defines evening civil twilight as the time that begins in the morning, or ends in the evening, when the
geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. Therefore, morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the
sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, and ends at sunrise. Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of
the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. The FAA has an online tool to calculate sunrise, sunset, and civil twilight for any given
location.

questions.question: According to the National Weather Service definition referenced in the Airplane Flying Handbook, evening civil twilight ends at what specific point?
questions.correct_answer: When the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon.
distractors: When the sun is no longer visible on the horizon.
When the geometric center of the sun is 12 degrees below the horizon.
At the beginning of morning civil twilight.
questions.explanation: The Airplane Flying Handbook, referencing 14 CFR part 1 and the National Weather Service, states that evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. This marks the beginning of 'night' as defined by the FAA.

reference.text:
According to 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1, Definitions and Abbreviations, “night” means the time between the end of evening civil
twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time. To explain further, the
National Weather Service defines evening civil twilight as the time that begins in the morning, or ends in the evening, when the
geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. Therefore, morning civil twilight begins when the geometric center of the
sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, and ends at sunrise. Evening civil twilight begins at sunset and ends when the geometric center of
the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon. The FAA has an online tool to calculate sunrise, sunset, and civil twilight for any given

questions.question: A pilot completes three takeoffs and landings to a full stop 30 minutes after sunset. Assuming the aircraft category and class are appropriate and the landings were within the preceding 90 days, do these landings satisfy the night currency requirement to carry passengers?
questions.correct_answer: No, because for night currency, the landings must occur between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise.
distractors: Yes, because night is defined as the period from sunset to sunrise.
No, because night currency requires the landings to occur at least 90 days prior to the flight.
Yes, because night is defined as the period from the end of evening civil twilight to the beginning of morning civil twilight.
questions.explanation: According to 14 CFR part 61, section 61.57(b)(1), as stated in the Airplane Flying Handbook, to act as PIC with passengers at night, the required three takeoffs and landings to a full stop must be performed during the time period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise. Landings performed 30 minutes after sunset do not meet this specific regulatory definition for night currency.

reference.text:
For 14 CFR part 61, section 61.57(b)(1) night operations that meet recent flight experience requirements, the term “night” refers to
the time period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise. The same regulation requires that during those hours,
no person may act as pilot-in-command (PIC) of an aircraft carrying passengers unless within the preceding 90 days and during those
specified hours, that person has made 3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop. 14 CFR part 61, sections 61.57(b)(1)(i) and (ii) require the
pilot to have made the required takeoffs and landings acting as the sole manipulator of the controls, and to have performed the
takeoffs and landings in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required). Other conditions apply if using a
full flight simulator to meet the requirement as described in 14 CFR part 61 (section 61.57(b)(2)) or if seeking to use another
alternative provided in the regulation.

questions.question: A pilot wants to carry passengers at night and is completing three takeoffs and landings to a full stop to meet recent flight experience requirements. Which statement correctly describes a requirement for how these takeoffs and landings must be performed?
questions.correct_answer: The pilot must have acted as the sole manipulator of the controls for each takeoff and landing
distractors: The pilot must have been officially designated as PIC for each takeoff and landing
The pilot must have been the only pilot aboard the aircraft during the takeoffs and landings
The pilot must have logged the flight time as PIC in their logbook for each takeoff and landing
questions.explanation: According to 14 CFR part 61, sections 61.57(b)(1)(i) and (ii), the pilot must have made the required takeoffs and landings acting as the sole manipulator of the controls, and in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required). Being designated as PIC, being the only pilot aboard, or logging PIC time are not the specific requirements stated in the regulation — the key requirement is being the sole manipulator of the controls.

reference.text:

alternative provided in the regulation.

questions.question: A pilot completed 3 full-stop landings at night 40 days ago in a multi-engine land airplane while acting as sole manipulator of the controls. The pilot now wishes to act as PIC carrying passengers at night in a single-engine land airplane. May the pilot do so based on those landings?
questions.correct_answer: No, because the landings were not performed in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required)
distractors: Yes, because both aircraft share the same category (airplane) and the landings were within the preceding 90 days
Yes, because the pilot acted as sole manipulator of the controls for all 3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop
No, because the landings must be performed in the same make and model of aircraft
questions.explanation: Per 14 CFR 61.57(b)(1), to act as PIC at night with passengers, a pilot must have made 3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop within the preceding 90 days acting as sole manipulator of the controls in an aircraft of the same category, class, and type (if a type rating is required). While the pilot met the 90-day, full-stop, and sole-manipulator requirements, the multi-engine land and single-engine land aircraft are different classes, so the currency does not transfer. Distractor 1 is wrong because category alone is insufficient—class must also match. Distractor 2 is wrong because sole manipulation is necessary but not sufficient without the same category/class/type. Distractor 3 is wrong because the requirement is category, class, and type—not make and model.

reference.text:

questions.question: A pilot has not flown at night in over 90 days and wants to carry passengers on a night flight. The pilot has access to a full flight simulator. Which statement is correct regarding meeting night currency requirements?
questions.correct_answer: A full flight simulator may be used to meet night currency requirements under conditions specified in 14 CFR 61.57(b)(2)
distractors: Only actual takeoffs and landings in an aircraft during night hours can satisfy the night currency requirement
A full flight simulator may be used, but only if the pilot first completes a flight review with a CFI
A full flight simulator may be used for instrument currency but is not permitted for night currency
questions.explanation: According to AFH Chapter 11, while 14 CFR 61.57(b)(1) requires a pilot to have made 3 takeoffs and landings to a full stop at night within the preceding 90 days to act as PIC carrying passengers, the regulation also provides that a full flight simulator may be used to meet this requirement under the conditions specified in 14 CFR 61.57(b)(2). The simulator is a valid alternative to actual flight for regaining night currency, provided the regulatory conditions are met.

questions.question: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook, why should pilots understand the physiology of the eye and how it functions in low-light conditions?
questions.correct_answer: Because vision involves the eyes and brain working together, and understanding this function enables pilots to adopt behaviors that significantly improve night vision.
distractors: Because understanding eye physiology allows pilots to self-diagnose and correct visual deficiencies before conducting night flights.
Because it helps pilots determine when to transition from visual flight rules to instrument flight rules during low-light conditions.
Because it allows pilots to identify and avoid permanent eye damage caused by prolonged exposure to low-light environments.
questions.explanation: The AFH (Chapter 11, Night Vision) states that because vision involves the eyes and brain working together, understanding eye function leads to pilot behaviors that can improve night vision significantly. The goal is not self-diagnosis, deciding when to fly IFR, or preventing eye damage — it is about adopting practical behaviors that compensate for the eye's diminished performance in low light.

reference.text:
Due to the physiology of the eye [Figure 11-1], humans experience diminished vision in low-light conditions. Because vision
involves the eyes and brain working together, understanding eye function leads to pilot behaviors that can improve night vision
significantly.

questions.question: In the human eye, what is the primary role of the cones located in the central area of the retina?
questions.correct_answer: They are involved with central vision to detect detail, perceive color, and identify far-away objects.
distractors: They are used for low-light vision and are highly sensitive to movement in the peripheral field of view.
They regulate the dilation of the pupil to adjust the amount of light entering the eye during high-intensity conditions.
They provide peripheral vision but sacrifice visual acuity and color perception to detect motion.
questions.explanation: According to the Airplane Flying Handbook (AFH) Chapter 11, cones are concentrated in the central area of the retina (the macula and fovea) and are used for day or high-intensity light vision. Their primary role is to facilitate central vision, allowing a pilot to detect fine detail, perceive color, and identify far-away objects. Distractors describing low-light vision, peripheral movement detection, or pupil regulation are functions of rods or the iris, not the cones.

reference.text:
⦁ The cones are located in higher concentrations than rods in the central area of the retina known as the
      macula, which measures about 4.5 mm in diameter. The exact center of the macula has a very small
      depression called the fovea, which contains cones only. The cones are used for day or high-intensity light
      vision. They are involved with central vision to detect detail, perceive color, and identify far-away objects.
